summary.title: ispc: A SPMD Compiler for High-Performance CPU Programming
summary.one_liner: ispc is a C-based SPMD compiler that maps program instances onto CPU SIMD lanes, and the paper explains its design goals, execution model, control-flow masking, and why gathers and scatters hurt CPU performance.
keywords: how to write simd code on cpu
array of structures vs structure of arrays
takeaways: ispc runs SPMD program instances across SIMD lanes, so code that looks scalar is vectorized by design rather than by heuristic.
Divergent control flow is handled by the compiler through masks and blend/select instructions, especially hard on SSE due to limited write-masks.
Non-contiguous array indexing becomes gathers and scatters, which CURRENT CPU hardware (SSE/AVX) implements as slower scalar instruction series.
Gang size is typically up to twice the SIMD width and is fixed at compile time, and the paper reports speedups up to 35x on 4 cores and 240x on 40 cores versus serial C++.
summary.summary: The paper presents ispc, an Intel compiler that extends a C-like language with SPMD constructs so each program instance maps to one SIMD lane on x86 CPUs using SSE or AVX. It sets out design goals (performance transparency, productivity, C/C++ interoperability), contrasts the approach with auto-vectorization and intrinsics, and explains how divergent control flow is converted to masked data flow. It also covers why gathers and scatters from non-contiguous memory access are costly on CPUs, which motivates ispc's layout and gather-minimization techniques. The excerpt ends before the detailed evaluation and layout sections, so the array-of-structures versus structure-of-arrays measurement is not visible in the provided text.
